newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German bourse set to boost Frankfurt's status.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German bourse set to boost Frankfurt's status.

text.p: The German bourse Deutsche Boerse AG has unveiled a scenario to boost Frankfurt's standing as a financial centre in a bid to propel it into the league of fully international trading centres with London and New York.

Deutsche Boerse chief executive Werner Seifert, presenting the plan to financial journalists on Tuesday evening, warned there was no time to lose in equipping Frankfurt to become a prime centre for trading in due course in the European single currency products.
The bourse was thus acting now to try to reach a select group of around 4,000 decision-makers in politics and industry, all of whom could take action to help the financial centre.
In a multi-pronged approach, it hoped to create a dynamic process which would make the market more accessible and more attractive to investors and companies alike.

Seifert argued that moves to reform outdated structures in Germany's economy should play into the bourse's hand, with planned pension and tax reforms ultimately having the effect of driving private investors' cash into a hungry share market.
"There are a lot of pressures for change at the moment that are going in our direction, giving us a tailwind," he said.

German private individuals are currently almost chronically under-invested in equities compared with their counterparts in Anglo-Saxon countries, holding only around six percent of their total assets in shares.

Tax breaks which favour other forms of investment, together with a state-financed pension system, have discouraged traditionally conservative German investors from plunging their savings into riskier equities.
Seifert argued that this would have to change as Germans were forced, and lured, into becaming more reliant on individual planning for retirement.

He admitted however that such change would not come overnight. Referring to the failure of the Bonn government so far to implement reforms, he said, "When we see how long it takes us to make decisions we realise that we have a problem."
Frankfurt was nonetheless already well-equipped for further expansion in securities trading, Seifert argued.

Trading costs on its IBIS computer system were low in international comparison and German bonds, or Bunds, were ideally positioned to take over as the benchmark under a single currency -- provided Bonn decided soon to convert all debt to euros from the currency's launch.
The bourse itself was preparing with new systems and products -- such as its "New Market" for small companies, and the planned XETRA conputer-based trading system.
It was also making concrete efforts to internationalise trading in Frankfurt, by extending trading times and looking to broaden the base of paper traded in the centre, he said.
One example was that it was considering trading contracts on the Dow Jones index over its systems, which would allow a pre-bourse trade on the index before U.S. markets open.

But Seifert conceded the market was still lacking in depth -- with many of Germany's smaller companies, the Mittelstand which forms the backbone of the economy, still under family ownership and shunning the idea of a bourse listing.

"What we need now is to convince some companies that a listing is a good way to raise capital," he said, adding this would provide a role for the regional bourses -- dotted across Germany in seven locations outside Frankfurt.

Asked what the future would be for these smaller bourses Siefert said he did not expect them simply to close down, even though it was clear that trade in major securities should be concentrated in Frankfurt.
"They will still have a role in convincing companies on the spot, in the region, that they should consider tapping the bourse for cash," he said.
